name: Syllogisms — All, Some and No, Made Certain
whatIsIt: A syllogism gives two statements about groups — using All, Some, or No — and asks which conclusion definitely follows. You decide using Venn circles: draw one circle per group and see which arrangements of the circles satisfy BOTH statements, then check if the conclusion is true in every one of those arrangements.
whyNeeded: Syllogisms train you to accept ONLY what is logically guaranteed, not what merely sounds likely — a skill exams reward heavily because most wrong answers are 'tempting but not certain'. A small set of memorized valid patterns makes these fast, sure marks.
realLifeUses: Reasoning sections of SSC, banking and railway exams
Spotting flawed 'therefore' arguments in news or ads
Legal and logical reasoning at any level of study
Careful, evidence-based thinking in everyday arguments

vocabulary.meaning: One of the two given statements (the facts you're told to accept as true).
The 'therefore' statement you're checking — does it definitely follow from the premises?
Overlapping circles, one per group, used to check every possible arrangement that fits the premises.
Reversing a statement (e.g. 'All B are A' from 'All A are B') — usually NOT automatically true.

story.title: The Cat and the Pet Shop
story.text: Nisha says: 'All cats are animals. Some animals are pets.' Dev quickly says, 'So some cats are pets!' Nisha stops him. 'Draw it,' she says. She sketches a big circle for Animals, a smaller circle for Cats fully inside it — that part's certain. But 'some animals are pets' could be pets that are dogs, birds, anything — the Pets circle could overlap Animals anywhere, even nowhere near Cats. 'We can't be SURE any cat is a pet,' she says. 'It's possible, but not guaranteed — so it doesn't follow.'
story.extractedProblem: All cats are animals. Some animals are pets. Does 'Some cats are pets' definitely follow?
story.answerInStory: No — the 'pets' circle can be drawn overlapping Animals without touching Cats at all, so the conclusion isn't guaranteed.

visual.caption: Picture three overlapping circles — draw every way they COULD overlap that still fits both sentences; only trust a conclusion true in every single drawing.

teachingGallery.title: The five memorable patterns
teachingGallery.note: These five combinations cover almost every syllogism you'll see — learn the shape of each, not just the words.

examples.caption: All A are B + All B are C → All A are C (a full chain — A sits entirely inside C).
All A are B + No B are C → No A are C (A is inside B, B and C never touch, so A and C never touch).
Some A are B + All B are C → Some A are C (the overlapping slice of A and B is entirely inside C too).

standardMethod.summary: Draw the two premises as Venn circles in every distinct way they could possibly be true together. Check the proposed conclusion against EVERY one of those drawings — it's valid only if it holds in all of them, not just the 'obvious' one.
steps: Draw the first premise's circles (e.g. All A are B → small A circle fully inside big B circle).
Add the second premise's circle in every possible position that still keeps the first premise true.
For each conclusion offered, check: is it true in EVERY possible drawing?
If yes in all drawings → conclusion follows. If it fails in even one possible drawing → it does not follow.

alternateMethods.name: Five valid patterns (memorized)
alternateMethods.whenToUse: Once you recognize the pattern, skip redrawing and apply it directly for speed.
steps: All A are B + All B are C → All A are C.
All A are B + No B are C → No A are C.
Some A are B + All B are C → Some A are C.
Some A are B + No B are C → Some A are not C.
Two negative or two 'some' premises together (e.g. No+No, or All+Some the wrong way) usually give NO valid conclusion — always double-check with a quick Venn sketch if unsure.
alternateMethods.example: All dogs are animals + All animals are living things → All dogs are living things (chain pattern).

workedExamples.problem: All roses are flowers. All flowers are plants. Conclusion: All roses are plants. Does it follow?
steps: This is the chain pattern: All A are B + All B are C.
Roses circle is fully inside Flowers circle, which is fully inside Plants circle.
So Roses is automatically fully inside Plants in every valid drawing.

workedExamples.problem: Some students are athletes. All athletes are disciplined. Conclusion: Some students are disciplined. Does it follow?
steps: Pattern: Some A are B + All B are C.
The overlapping students-athletes slice is part of Athletes, which is entirely inside Disciplined.
So that overlapping slice of students is also inside Disciplined — some students are disciplined, guaranteed.

workedExamples.problem: No fish are mammals. No mammals are reptiles. Conclusion: No fish are reptiles. Does it follow?
steps: Pattern: No A are B + No B are C — this is the 'two negatives' case.
Fish avoids Mammals, and Mammals avoids Reptiles, but Fish and Reptiles could still overlap freely, or not at all — nothing pins it down.
You can draw a valid picture where Fish and Reptiles DO overlap, and another where they don't — so the conclusion isn't guaranteed.

trickPractice.trick: Match the shape, not the words
trickPractice.intro: Recognize which of the five patterns you're looking at, then apply its known result instantly.

questions.q: All A are B. All B are C. Conclusion: All A are C.
All A are B. Conclusion: All B are A.
hintLadder: B could be bigger than A.

questions.q: Some A are B. No B are C. Conclusion: Some A are not C.
hintLadder: The A-B overlap avoids C entirely.
So that overlapping part of A is definitely outside C.
Some A are not C — follows.

questions.q: No A are B. No B are C. Conclusion: No A are C.
hintLadder: A and C aren't pinned down at all.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming 'All A are B' also means 'All B are A' (treating the statement as reversible).
commonMistakes.fix: 'All A are B' only guarantees A is inside B — B can easily be a bigger circle with room outside A. Never reverse an 'All' statement automatically.

commonMistakes.mistake: Concluding something definite from two 'No' statements, or from a 'No' plus a loosely related 'Some' statement, when actually nothing is guaranteed.
commonMistakes.fix: Two negative (or otherwise weakly connected) premises usually leave the third group's position completely free — sketch a quick Venn diagram to check before trusting any 'obvious' conclusion.

commonMistakes.mistake: Missing that 'Some A are B' + 'No B are C' gives a valid but easy-to-miss conclusion: 'Some A are NOT C' (not 'Some A are C').
commonMistakes.fix: When the second premise is 'No', the valid conclusion about the outer group is always a NEGATIVE 'some are not', never a positive 'some are'.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming 'All A are B' + 'Some B are C' guarantees 'Some A are C', by assuming the B-C overlap must land inside A.
commonMistakes.fix: Only the reverse chains: 'Some A are B' + 'All B are C' gives 'Some A are C'. With 'All A are B' + 'Some B are C', the C-overlap could sit entirely in the part of B that has no A — no valid conclusion follows.

commonMistakes.mistake: Chaining 'Some A are B' with 'Some B are C' as if both point to the same slice of B, giving 'Some A are C'.
commonMistakes.fix: Two 'Some' statements can describe completely different parts of B — nothing links the A-side overlap to the C-side overlap, so no valid conclusion follows from two 'Some' premises alone.

easy.q: All dogs are animals. All animals are living things. Conclusion: All dogs are living things.
hintLadder: Dogs inside Animals inside Living things.

easy.q: All squares are rectangles. Conclusion: All rectangles are squares.
Some birds are parrots. All parrots can talk (in this puzzle). Conclusion: Some birds can talk.
hintLadder: Some A are B, All B are C pattern.
Overlap of birds/parrots is inside 'can talk'.

medium.q: All pens are tools. No tools are toys. Conclusion: No pens are toys.
hintLadder: All A are B, No B are C pattern.
Pens fully inside Tools, Tools avoids Toys.

medium.q: Some teachers are singers. No singers are shy. Conclusion: Some teachers are not shy.
hintLadder: Some A are B, No B are C pattern.
Some teachers are not shy — follows.

medium.q: No apples are vegetables. Some vegetables are green. Conclusion: No apples are green.
hintLadder: Apples avoid Vegetables entirely, that's separate from 'green'.
Apples could still be green through another path.

challenge.q: All A are B. Some B are C. Conclusion: Some A are C.
hintLadder: A is inside B, but the B-C overlap could sit in the part of B without any A.
So A and C might never touch.

challenge.q: Some A are B. Some B are C. Conclusion: Some A are C.
hintLadder: The A-B overlap and B-C overlap need not be the same slice of B.

challenge.q: All A are B. No B are C. What is the strongest valid conclusion about A and C (one word: 'No' or 'Some')?
hintLadder: So A never touches C: 'No A are C'.

questions.q: All mangoes are fruits. All fruits are food. Conclusion: All mangoes are food.
All cats are pets. Conclusion: All pets are cats.
Some pens are red. All red things are bright. Conclusion: Some pens are bright.
hintLadder: Some A are B, All B are C pattern.

questions.q: No snakes are birds. No birds are fish. Conclusion: No snakes are fish.
hintLadder: Snakes and fish are left unpinned.

questions.q: Some doctors are writers. No writers are lazy. Conclusion: Some doctors are not lazy.
hintLadder: Some A are B, No B are C pattern.
Some doctors are not lazy — follows.

teachBackPrompt: Teach a friend why 'All cats are animals, some animals are pets' does NOT guarantee 'some cats are pets' — draw the three circles and show a valid arrangement where it's false.

revisionCard.summary: Trust only what's true in EVERY possible Venn-circle drawing of the premises, not just the 'obvious' one. Five patterns to memorize: All+All chains (All A are C); All+No stays No (No A are C); Some+All chains partly (Some A are C); Some+No gives a negative (Some A are not C); two negatives (or All+Some the wrong way round) usually give no valid conclusion. Never assume 'All A are B' reverses to 'All B are A'.

gameMission.title: The Overlapping Circles
gameMission.brief: Test every possible way the jungle animal-groups could overlap — only trust conclusions that hold true in ALL of them!

realLifeProject: Write two of your own All/Some/No statements about things around your house, then draw the Venn circles to work out what conclusion (if any) definitely follows.

rememberIt.hook: True in every drawing, or it doesn't follow
rememberIt.unpack: A conclusion is valid only if it holds in EVERY possible Venn-circle arrangement of the premises.

studentQuestions.q: Why can't I just trust the conclusion that 'sounds right'?
studentQuestions.a: Because syllogisms are about logical certainty, not likelihood — an answer that's merely probable, but not guaranteed by the premises, is a trap exams deliberately include.

studentQuestions.q: Is there a shortcut once I know the five patterns?
studentQuestions.a: Yes — once you can instantly recognize which of the five shapes (All+All, All+No, Some+All, Some+No, or the two 'no-conclusion' cases) a question matches, you can answer in seconds without redrawing circles every time.
